EXTENSION OF EFFECTIVE DATE OF REQUIRE­
MENT FOR CARRIAGE OF CRASH AX(ES)  
ABOARD SCHEDULED AIR CARRIER AIRPLANES
Adopted by the Civil Aeronautics 
Board at its office in Washington, D. C., 
on the 29th day of December 1954.
Section 40.173 (d) of Part 40 of the 
Civil Air Regulations requires that “On 
and after January 1, 1955, all airplanes 
shall be equipped with at least one crash 
ax, and if accommodations are provided 
for more than 30 persons including the 
crew, airplanes shall be equipped with at 
least two crash axes. This equipment 
shall be stowed in readily accessible loca­
tions.”
The Air Transport Association has 
recently requested that further study be 
made prior to the implementation of 
this requirement. Questions have been 
raised as to the effectiveness: of a crash 
ax for cutting through the fuselage of an 
airplane and, particularly, to the advis­
ability from a safety standpoint of
stowing a crash ax in the passenger com­
partment of the airplane.
The Bureau of Safety Regulation has 
been conducting an investigation into 
the question of the need for a crash ax 
as an article of emergency equipment for 
all air carrier operations. Data received 
from the air forces concerning tests 
which were conducted by them indicated 
that the crash kit, which included a 
crash ax, was inadequate for the purpose 
for which it was intended. More re­
cently the NACA has conducted a series 
of tests in order to determine the effec­
tiveness of the crash ax in cutting an 
opening in an airplane fuselage through 
which passengers could be evacuated in 
an emergency. On the basis of these 
tests it appeared doubtful whether the 
average passenger could chop an ade­
quate opening through the fuselage by 
means of an ax. Furthermore, it was 
concluded that the opening would have 
to be sufficient in size to permit the pas­
senger to step through to the ground be­
cause of the sharp jagged edges resulting 
from the use of an ax. In fact, the mili’- 
tary has required that the ax be sup­
plemented by additional equipment such 
as a saw or a six pound sledge hammer 
in order to cope with the jagged edges.
In view of the foregoing information, 
the justification for a requirement for an 
ax for the use of passengers would ap­
pear to be somewhat uncertain. This 
is particularly true of the provision for a 
second ax on larger airplanes. There­
fore the Board feels that additional in­
vestigation of the problem is in order 
prior to making final disposition of the 
crash ax requirement. Inasmuch as this 
requirement is so closely allied with the 
requirement for chop marks on the fuse­
lage, the crash ax requirement will be 
extended to coincide with the April 1, 
1955, effective date for “chop marks.”
Interested persons have been afforded 
an opportunity to participate in the mak­
ing of this amendment, and due consid­
eration has been given to all relevant 
matter presented.
In consideration of the foregoing, the 
Civil Aeronautics Board hereby amends 
Part 40 of the Civil Air Regulations (14

operative_clauses.judgment_reason: First end 1955-01-31 (midnight closing that day) by the President's designation in EO 10585, which designates January 31, 1955 as the date of termination of combatant activities in the zone described in EO 10195. The designation of the zone and its commencement date are the order's only commands, and they operate only for the period ending on that date. The held OFR cross-reference lists the instrument date Jan. 1, 1955, which is not the termination date.

research_rationale:
EO 10195 (Dec. 20, 1950; 15 FR 9177) designated Korea and the adjacent waters within stated limits as a combat zone under section 22(b)(13) of the Internal Revenue Code (as amended by the Revenue Act of 1950) and fixed June 27, 1950 as the date combatant activities commenced there. EO 10585 (signed Jan. 1, 1955; 20 FR 17) was issued under section 112(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 and designates January 31, 1955, as of midnight thereof, as the date of termination of combatant activities in the zone comprised of the area described in EO 10195. The OFR note points to EO 10585 with the signing date Jan. 1, 1955, but that is the date of the instrument; the termination date it designates is January 31, 1955. A combat-zone designation exists only for the period between the commencement date and the termination date, so the designation ended at midnight closing 1955-01-31 (inclusive reading; the exclusive reading is that it ended when Feb. 1, 1955 began). EO 10195 has no own-terms end and no other held instrument revokes or amends it; EO 10585 is the only later instrument naming it. Residual (see also the held Combat Duty Pay Act of 1952, sec. 702(f), which incorporates the EO 10195 area by reference as its own statutory definition): tax consequences for service within June 27, 1950 to Jan. 31, 1955 accrued and are a surviving effect of the designation rather than a continuing command.
Member checks: {"earlier_end_check":"Searched the held corpus for citations of Executive Order 10195 by number: six held files cite it (EO 10585, the Federal Register page, a 1952 Public Law citing the zone and the 1989 OFR codification text). Only EO 10585 acts on the zone. The order has no own-terms expiry; the until and effective signals in the text come from neighbouring documents on the same Federal Register page. The current-law searches (U.S. Code and eCFR) had no hit naming EO 10195.","independent_command_check":"No clause is independent: the commencement date only fixes the start of the period over which the designation runs, and ends with it. A later statutory or tax rule that refers to the zone by period or area (for example the Combat Duty Pay Act of 1952, Title VII of Public Law 488, sec. 702(f), which defines Korea by reference to EO 10195) is a separate effect (see savings), not a command of EO 10195.","savings_check":"See savings_reason.","scope_check":"The order is one paragraph with two designations: the area (Korea and adjacent waters) and the commencement date. EO 10585 terminates combatant activities in the zone comprised of the area described in EO 10195, so the area designation is spent as of the termination date; the commencement date is the start of the period and has no independent forward command. The clause inventory keeps the single whole-order clause."}

savings_residuals.reason: The designation operated for the period June 27, 1950 through the termination date. The tax-exclusion consequences that attached to service in the zone during that period (and the 1952 public law text held in the corpus that defines Korea by reference to EO 10195) are accrued effects of a completed designation. EO 10585 does not cancel them and no held source shows a continuing command in EO 10195. Held statute text: the Combat Duty Pay Act of 1952 (Title VII of Public Law 488, July 10, 1952, 66 Stat. 538-539, section 702(f), in jobs/source-ladder/output/texts/queue_EO_10394_Pub._L._504_82d_Cong._sec._103_Civil_Functions_Appropriation_Act_1953_and_Pub._L._488_3065af7aab.txt) defines "Korea" as the geographical area specified for income-tax-exemption purposes by Executive Order 10195, approved December 20, 1950. This is a statutory definition that adopts the area as it stood when enacted; it is the statute's own command (combat pay at $45 per month for months after May 31, 1950), not a command of EO 10195, so it neither continues the designation nor is ended by EO 10585. The statute does not alter EO 10195 or EO 10585.

EXTENSION OF EFFECTIVE DATE OF REQUIRE­
MENT FOR CARRIAGE OF CRASH AX(ES)  
ABOARD SCHEDULED AIR CARRIER AIRPLANES
Adopted by the Civil Aeronautics 
Board at its office in Washington, D. C., 
on the 29th day of December 1954.
Section 40.173 (d) of Part 40 of the 
Civil Air Regulations requires that “On 
and after January 1, 1955, all airplanes 
shall be equipped with at least one crash 
ax, and if accommodations are provided 
for more than 30 persons including the 
crew, airplanes shall be equipped with at 
least two crash axes. This equipment 
shall be stowed in readily accessible loca­
tions.”
The Air Transport Association has 
recently requested that further study be 
made prior to the implementation of 
this requirement. Questions have been 
raised as to the effectiveness: of a crash 
ax for cutting through the fuselage of an 
airplane and, particularly, to the advis­
ability from a safety standpoint of
stowing a crash ax in the passenger com­
partment of the airplane.
The Bureau of Safety Regulation has 
been conducting an investigation into 
the question of the need for a crash ax 
as an article of emergency equipment for 
all air carrier operations. Data received 
from the air forces concerning tests 
which were conducted by them indicated 
that the crash kit, which included a 
crash ax, was inadequate for the purpose 
for which it was intended. More re­
cently the NACA has conducted a series 
of tests in order to determine the effec­
tiveness of the crash ax in cutting an 
opening in an airplane fuselage through 
which passengers could be evacuated in 
an emergency. On the basis of these 
tests it appeared doubtful whether the 
average passenger could chop an ade­
quate opening through the fuselage by 
means of an ax. Furthermore, it was 
concluded that the opening would have 
to be sufficient in size to permit the pas­
senger to step through to the ground be­
cause of the sharp jagged edges resulting 
from the use of an ax. In fact, the mili’- 
tary has required that the ax be sup­
plemented by additional equipment such 
as a saw or a six pound sledge hammer 
in order to cope with the jagged edges.
In view of the foregoing information, 
the justification for a requirement for an 
ax for the use of passengers would ap­
pear to be somewhat uncertain. This 
is particularly true of the provision for a 
second ax on larger airplanes. There­
fore the Board feels that additional in­
vestigation of the problem is in order 
prior to making final disposition of the 
crash ax requirement. Inasmuch as this 
requirement is so closely allied with the 
requirement for chop marks on the fuse­
lage, the crash ax requirement will be 
extended to coincide with the April 1, 
1955, effective date for “chop marks.”
Interested persons have been afforded 
an opportunity to participate in the mak­
ing of this amendment, and due consid­
eration has been given to all relevant 
matter presented.
In consideration of the foregoing, the 
Civil Aeronautics Board hereby amends
